name: Beth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the phones for an airline's bookings line, out at a contact centre by the airport. I log in at seven, and the first hour is always people whose flights got cancelled overnight, so it's rebooking, rebooking, rebooking. I like the puzzle of it, finding someone a seat through another city when the system says there's nothing. What wears me out is the shouting, especially on bank holiday weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's your life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years this spring. I live with Owen, my partner, he's an electrician, and we rent a two-bed near the ring road. I've got about ten months of pay put away and my car's paid off, because I'm careful like that. My mum always said keep a year in the bank and you'll sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year there's a new system they swear will change everything, and we end up phoning the customer back anyway. I'd probably say it at break to Dawn, who sits next to me, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and my weekends stay the same. The airline might use the AI to send out the cancellation texts faster, which would actually help me. I don't really see a downside, apart from maybe fewer overtime shifts in the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep putting three hundred a month into savings, and maybe go for the team leader trainee spot when it comes up next year. I'd skip any optional AI training if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything. It's the version where I don't have to change anything I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip the AI training. What if they made it part of your review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I'm not daft. I'd sit through it and pass the quiz, same as I did with the new booking screens two years ago. But I wouldn't go out of my way to use it on calls if I didn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already pressing on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent went up again in March, and Owen and I want to buy somewhere in a couple of years. That's the main thing on my mind. But with both our wages and my savings, it feels doable if nothing big changes.

say: I'd say the **AI talk** was mostly hype, like every new system before it.
I'd keep it to a **break-room chat** with Dawn rather than posting anything online.
think: My **job and weekends** stay the same, and faster cancellation texts would actually help me.
The only real loss might be fewer **winter overtime** shifts.
do: Keep working my shifts and saving **£300 a month** towards a house deposit.
Apply for the **team leader trainee** spot when it opens next year.
Sit any required **AI training** but avoid using it on live calls.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, because nothing I'm good at has to change.
S0.quote: Every year there's a new system they swear will change everything, and we end up phoning the customer back anyway.
fieldNote: Beth's **steadiness** comes from savings habits learned from her mother, not from confidence in the airline.
She'd comply with AI training only when forced, a clear **resistant** streak.
Her real pressure is **rent and a house**, and she feels on top of it here.

steps.text: Keep saving 300 a month towards a house deposit with Owen
Apply for the team leader trainee spot at the bookings centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my head down and say we'll see. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't post about work. With friends I'd probably say the airline has been trying to get rid of us for years and now it's found a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, rebooking is exactly the kind of thing a computer could do once it can talk. Most of my calls are the same twenty problems. A bot that rebooks people at three in the morning means no night shift, then half of us gone on days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager, Gary, straight out which roles are staying. I'd look at jobs at the airport itself, the check-in desks or the lost baggage office, because that's still face to face. And I'd stop spending on anything big, no holiday this year, and keep the deposit money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, a bit. I've been good at this job and it's horrible thinking good doesn't count anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the check-in desk and not, say, learning the new bot and staying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it. The people who learn the bot will be training their own replacement, and I've watched that happen with the self-service kiosks at the airport. At least at a check-in desk there's a person standing in front of you who needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Owen talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we still buy the house. Owen would say his work is fine, nobody's automating rewiring a kitchen. He'd be right, but I'd still want to wait a year before signing a mortgage on my half of the wages.

say: I'd tell friends the airline has **wanted us gone** for years and now has a way.
At work I'd stay quiet and say **we'll see**, and I'd post nothing online.
think: Most of my calls are the **same twenty problems**, which a talking computer could handle.
Losing the **night shift** first would be a sign that half the day team goes next.
do: Ask my manager Gary **which roles stay** in the bookings team.
Look at **check-in and baggage** desk jobs at the airport itself.
Cancel this year's holiday and leave the **deposit money** untouched.
feel: A **tight chest**, because being good at the job might stop counting.
S1.quote: Most of my calls are the same twenty problems. A bot that rebooks people at three in the morning means no night shift, then half of us gone on days.
fieldNote: Beth's distrust of AI is **personal**: she watched airport kiosks replace desk staff.
She'd move **sideways** into face-to-face work rather than learn the new tools.
Owen's **secure trade** steadies her, but she still delays the mortgage.

steps.text: Ask Gary which roles in the bookings team will stay
Apply for check-in or lost baggage desk jobs at the airport
Cancel this year's holiday and leave the deposit savings alone
Put off signing a mortgage for at least a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should have stopped it. I'm not political, but two years is no time at all. At work everyone would be saying the same, so I'd just be one more voice in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job's gone, probably within a year of it arriving. Phones and chat are pure thinking work, nothing hands-on about it. A check-in desk buys me maybe three years until the robots come. And that's if the airline still wants a human face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast, which isn't like me. I'd ask Owen whether his firm would take me on as an apprentice electrician, because that's hands-on and he says there's a shortage. I'd keep every penny of savings, and I'd stop paying into the deposit and just hold cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I keep thinking of my mum's line about a year in the bank, and wondering if a year is enough when everything moves at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving fast isn't like you. What would actually get you to sign up for an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first redundancy letters go out on my floor. I'm not someone who jumps early, I'd need to see it. But I'd have the forms filled in and sitting in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robots come for electrical work three years after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have had three more years of wages, which is something. I don't have an answer past that. Nobody I know does.

say: I'd call it **madness** that nobody slowed it down.
In the canteen I'd be just **one more voice** saying the same thing.
think: Phones and chat are **pure thinking work**, so my job likely goes within a year.
An airport desk only buys me about **three years** before robots arrive.
do: Ask Owen whether his firm takes on an **apprentice electrician**.
Stop paying into the deposit and **hold cash** instead.
Fill in apprenticeship forms early but wait for the first **redundancy letters**.
feel: Properly **scared**, wondering whether a year of savings is enough when everything moves at once.
S2.quote: Phones and chat are pure thinking work, nothing hands-on about it. A check-in desk buys me maybe three years until the robots come.
fieldNote: Beth sees the **thinking-first** timing clearly and knows her job sits right in its path.
Even alarmed, she won't act until she sees **redundancy letters**, which fits her resistance.
Owen's **electrical trade** is her only escape route, and she knows it's temporary.

steps.text: Ask Owen whether his firm would take her on as an apprentice electrician
Stop paying into the house deposit and keep all savings as cash
Fill in apprenticeship forms and wait for the first redundancy letters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not panic. I'd probably share the news story in the family group chat and say this is what I've been worried about. Dawn would say I'm being dramatic, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is about the length of time I've been doing this job. So it's like being told this job ends when I'd have been here ten years. I'd still be under forty when the robots come, which is worse in a way, because there's a whole working life left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in electrical installation at the college, two nights a week, while still on the phones. I'd keep saving, but I'd also buy the house sooner than later, because a mortgage gets harder once you've lost a steady job. Owen and I would sit down with the bank this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a low hum. Not the panic of the two-year one, but it wouldn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying the house sooner is a big step for someone who likes to wait. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because banks want payslips. If I wait until I'm retraining on an apprentice wage, nobody will lend to us. My dad lost his job at the print works when I was twelve, and my parents never got a mortgage after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dawn, actually. She's forty-six and has two kids and she won't retrain, she's said so. She's been doing phones for twenty years and it's all she knows.

say: I'd say there are **a few years**, so nobody should panic yet.
I'd share the **news story** in the family chat as proof of my worry.
think: Five years is about my **time in the job**, so it ends at ten years.
I'd still be **under forty** when robots arrive, with a whole working life left.
do: Start an **evening course** in electrical installation, two nights a week.
Meet the bank with Owen this year to **buy the house** while payslips are steady.
Keep saving while still working **on the phones**.
feel: A low, **constant unease**, quieter than panic but never fully gone.
S3.quote: My dad lost his job at the print works when I was twelve, and my parents never got a mortgage after that.
fieldNote: Her father's **job loss** drives her urge to lock in a mortgage while payslips last.
With five years, the usually cautious Beth **starts retraining early** in the evenings.
She worries most for **Dawn**, a long-serving colleague who won't retrain.

steps.text: Start a two-night-a-week electrical installation course at the college
Meet the bank with Owen and buy the house this year
Keep the bookings job and keep saving each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. That's what I'd tell my mum, anyway, so she doesn't worry. At work I'd say the airline will probably go bust before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't hide in this job until I retire, but I don't have to jump tomorrow either. Ten years is enough to learn a trade properly and do it for a while. I think I'd be all right, if I actually got on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the phones job for another three or four years and save hard, maybe four hundred a month. I'd buy the house with Owen in the next two years. Then around year four I'd start the electrical course, and use the last years to build up hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not happy about it, but it feels like something I could plan for, like a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right if you actually got on with it. Do you think you would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest question. I'm the type to leave things until they're urgent. With ten years I might tell myself there's always next year, and then suddenly it's year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start on time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, probably. He's the one who would nag me. And if the airline cut the night shift early, that would be my alarm clock.

say: I'd tell my mum **ten years** is long enough that she needn't worry.
At work I'd joke the airline will **go bust** before the robots arrive.
think: I can't **hide in this job** until retirement, but I needn't jump tomorrow.
My real risk is that I **put it off** until year eight.
do: Stay on the phones three or four more years and save **£400 a month**.
Buy the house with Owen **within two years**.
Start the **electrical course** around year four and build up hours after.
feel: Calmer, because it feels like something I can **plan for**, like a pension.
S4.quote: I'm the type to leave things until they're urgent. With ten years I might tell myself there's always next year, and then suddenly it's year eight.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Beth's fear into a **timetable** she can live with.
She openly names her own **procrastination** as the biggest risk here.
A night-shift cut would be her **trigger** to act, with Owen pushing her.

steps.text: Stay on the airline phones and save 400 a month
Buy a house with Owen within the next two years
Start an electrical installation course around the fourth year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's the one where being careful doesn't save you, because there's no time to be careful. What would help is the airline giving us real notice and paying for retraining in a trade, not just sending us on a course about the new software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether we'd want to stay, even if they kept us. I like the puzzle bit of the job. If the bot does the puzzles and I just do the angry customers it can't handle, I'm not sure I'd want to stay anyway.

headlineQuote: If the bot does the puzzles and I just do the angry customers it can't handle, I'm not sure I'd want to stay anyway.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** airline bookings agent who loves the puzzle of rebooking stranded passengers.
She's careful with money, with **ten months saved**, and lives with Owen, an electrician.
She avoids AI tools and trusts **face-to-face work** more than any new system.
She moves from calm to **alarmed**, with an electrician apprenticeship as her escape route.
She knows her habit of **waiting too long** is her biggest weakness.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to be careful.
whatWouldHelp: Real **notice** from the airline and **paid retraining** in a trade, not software courses.
